findings.title: The fixed 30 s gap threshold wipes out all CPU time at cadences the configuration accepts, and in `submeter top --seconds 31..60`
findings.evidence: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py:39 gap_after_s=30.0; :55 gap = ... elapsed > self._gap_after_s ...; :67 cpu_busy_s=0.0 if gap; :78-79 every process cpu_s=0.0 when gap. core/config.py:45-50 idle_interval 1s-60s, cold_interval 5s-60s; :92 on_battery_multiplier up to 10. config.py has no gap setting. cli.py:79 top --seconds max=60.0, cli.py:87 Sampler() with the default. Probe gap_rule.out.txt section 1 (all accepted by config): 'idle_interval = 31s ... 20 of 20 ticks called a gap, 0% of the CPU time credited'; the same for 60 s idle, battery x2 with idle 16 s (32 s), battery x7 with the default idle 5 s (35 s), battery x10 (50 s), battery x4 with active 8 s (32 s), cold_interval 60 s. Section 3: a 35 s stall with both clocks running: 'the process used 17.50 CPU-s, credited 0.00, machine busy recorded 0.00'. Section 4: 'submeter top --seconds 31 --json ... 449 processes over 31.2 s; CPU time reported in total: 0.00 s'.
findings.impact: docs/17 Collection promises that 'a change of cadence never loses or invents CPU time'. Any interval over 30 s drops every process's CPU and the machine's busy time to zero. Such an interval comes from an accepted setting, from the on-battery multiplier, or from the overhead guard ('slow the cadence', which docs/08 calls for and which a psutil fallback needs: measured 95 ms per tick for 300 processes at 1%). Attribution, trends and the reconciliation all read zero for those periods. A stall where both clocks keep running is not a suspend, yet its CPU is still discarded.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/collector/sampler.py: never zero CPU or I/O deltas. Cumulative counters make them exact even across a suspend, because a suspended process accrues nothing. Use the gap flag only to mark the interval as unobserved for coverage and rates. Detect a suspend from wall - monotonic > slack. For a stall, compare elapsed with the scheduled interval passed in to ingest(), for example elapsed > 3 x scheduled + slack, not with a fixed 30 s. src/submeter/cli.py top: pass the scheduled interval. docs/05 step 3: state the rule in one sentence. Add a test with a 60 s interval and one with a 35 s stall.
findings.cost: About 15 lines in sampler.py and cli.py, two tests, one sentence in docs/05.
findings.refutation_attempt: I looked for a gap setting in config.py and for any caller that passes gap_after_s; there is none, and cli.py:87 uses the default. I checked whether the collector design caps intervals at 30 s: docs/08 allows 60 s and a multiplier of 10. I reran the logic in gap_rule.py, which feeds the real Sampler and runs the real `top`. R08's fix (record gaps) exists but treats every long interval as a gap.

findings.title: Gap intervals are rolled up as covered, idle time, so a suspend reads as an hour of near-zero use
findings.evidence: core/models.py:135-147 WorkloadSample has no gap field; attribution/rules.py:221 interval_s=batch.interval_s (for a gap batch that is max(elapsed, wall), sampler.py:59); store/raw.py:95-128 writes workload_raw rows for gap batches as well as the gap row; store/rollup.py:53 covered_s += interval with no gap check, and :110 puts the whole sample in the bucket that holds its midpoint. Probe gap_rule.out.txt section 2, a 1-hour suspend: 'minute bucket + 1800 s: covered 3601 s of 60, cpu 0.00 s, well covered True, cores p50 0.005'; 'hour bucket + 0 s: covered 3602 s of 3600 ... mean cores 0.0001 (the process used 0.5 while awake)'. docs/06:38 says buckets keep covered seconds 'so a gap is never read as zero use'.
findings.impact: Each suspend or stall becomes one bucket that claims more coverage than its width and shows zero use. It passes well_covered(), so baselines, the slow-growth check and time-weighted means take it as real idle time. The neighbouring buckets lose that coverage. This is the defect that R24 and R08 list as fixed.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/attribution/rules.py aggregate(): for a gap batch, emit workload rows with interval_s=0, or add WorkloadSample.gap and have rollup.py SeriesAccumulator.add() skip gap samples while still summing cpu_s. src/submeter/store/raw.py: write only the gap row for a gap batch. Add a test that a bucket containing a gap has covered_s <= width_s and that the gap is not counted as covered.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched src/ for any reader of the gap table that subtracts gaps from coverage: only raw.py writes it, and rollup.py never reads it. test_baseline.py:404-418 checks only that a gap row exists, not what the rollup does with it.

findings.title: Hot and cold sets cannot be expressed in the sampler's data model: either 68% of CPU is lost or a workload shows more cores than the machine has
findings.evidence: core/models.py: SampleBatch has one interval_s, and ProcessSample has no interval of its own. sampler.py:84-87: an old process that reappears is 'first seen' and credited 0. Probe hot_cold_sampler.out.txt, a synthetic 271-process machine at 1.58 cores in use: (A) hot-only snapshots between full ones: 'credited 30.0 CPU-s of 94.8 (32%), processes started 1620, exited 1620 (truth: 0 and 0)', 'memory min 0.10 GiB, max 26.46 GiB'. (B) cold counters carried forward and refreshed every 10th tick: total exact, but 'tick 10: 271 processes, 11.30 cores' on 8 logical cores, 'cores p95 11.62 (truth 1.58 both)'. docs/17 Collection: 'Every sample records the interval it covers'. docs/05:45 'hot set every 1 s and the cold set every 10 s'.
findings.impact: Build-list item 3 (hot and cold sets) cannot be built on the existing sampler without wrong numbers. Either CPU is lost and process start and exit counts are invented, or per-tick cores in use, percentiles and spike detection see 10 s of cold CPU divided by a 1 s interval. The cost model's savings (see the overhead finding) depend on this split.
findings.proposed_change: Choice below. Option 1, recommended: read every process's CPU every tick. The Windows bulk call returns all processes anyway, and a Linux stat-only read measured 7.5 ms per 300 processes. Apply the cold cadence only to the costly fields (memory detail, I/O, command line) and to row writing. State this in docs/05 step 2 and docs/17 Collection. Option 2: add interval_s and the previous read time to each ProcessSample, keep per-process last-read state in the sampler, and compute workload rates over bucket time rather than per tick.
findings.cost: Option 1: two sentences in docs/05 and docs/17, nothing in the baseline. Option 2: a model change of about 30 lines plus tests.
findings.decision_question: Should the cold set skip only the costly per-process fields, with CPU read for every process every tick, or should each process carry its own sampling interval? Recommendation: CPU every tick for all processes.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/05, docs/08 and docs/17 for how a mixed-interval tick is aggregated: nothing says. I checked whether Sampler keeps per-process state across snapshots: it keeps only the last snapshot (sampler.py:47-49). I ran both plausible ways of feeding the baseline sampler.

findings.title: The cost model in docs/08 underestimates the measured per-process cost by 4 to 24 times, and its 'in budget' row is over budget
findings.evidence: docs/08 assumes 1.5 ms + 0.012 ms per process, plus 0.2 points for the store and API, and 90 bytes per row. Measured on this machine (model_tables.out.txt section 3, from docs/review/probes/measure): psutil snapshot 0.2488 ms per process (20.7x); direct /proc stat+statm+io 0.0517 ms (4.3x); baseline whole tick 0.2817 ms (23.5x); raw store about 15.9 ms per tick at 447 processes (about 10.6 ms at 300, about 1.06 points at 1 s). collector_footprint: '14.1% of one core' at 1 s with 447 processes; '120 bytes per sample row'. The explorer recomputed with measured costs, 300 processes: whole tick + raw store 36.0 ms is 3.60% at 1 s (over); with the psutil fallback 95.1 ms it is 9.51% at 1 s and 1.90% at the 5 s idle interval (over 1%). docs/08 row '1 s, 10 s, 300: 0.7% In budget'. All 11 docs/08 rows reproduce exactly from its own formulas (model_tables section 2).
findings.impact: The P1 gate '30-minute CI soak stays inside the budget' fails with the baseline provider: 14.1% against 3%. Even a direct /proc reader with the raw store is over 3% at a 1 s active interval unless only a hot set is handled each tick (10% hot: 0.68%). The psutil fallback, which docs/17 makes part of the Windows design, cannot meet the 1% idle limit at 5 s. The explorer's table steers settings with figures 4 to 24 times too optimistic. The budget does not say whether the server's CPU counts, or how many processes a CI runner must hold.
findings.proposed_change: docs/08 'Sample time explorer': replace the assumed costs with the measured Linux figures above, labelled by provider and by part of the tick. Mark Windows as unmeasured until P0. Add a row for the psutil fallback. docs/17 'Overhead budget': say the CPU limit covers the collector process only (or collector plus server), measured as process CPU time over the soak with the load generator holding 300 processes.
findings.cost: About 15 lines in docs/08 and one sentence in docs/17.
findings.refutation_attempt: I recomputed the docs/08 formulas to make sure the table matches its own model: it does, so the gap lies in the assumptions, not the arithmetic. I used only the quiet-machine timings already taken, scaled linearly from 447 to 300 processes; per-process cost is roughly linear. Windows costs may differ, so the Windows claim is left open.

findings.title: The Rust switching rule in docs/11 is undefined and disagrees with the budget; applied to the measurements it gives a different answer per reading
findings.evidence: docs/11:69-70 'One full sample of 300 processes takes more than 10 ms', 'The collector process holds more than 80 MB'. model_tables.out.txt section 4: psutil snapshot 74.6 ms -> switch; direct /proc stat only 7.5 ms -> stay; stat+statm+io 15.5 ms -> switch; baseline tick 84.5 ms -> switch; collector memory resident 39 MB, unique 35, proportional 36 -> stay. '10 ms per sample is 1.0% of a core at 1 s and 0.2% at 5 s; the budget itself allows 30 ms per tick at 1 s (3%) and 50 ms per tick at 5 s (1%)'. docs/11:55 'its cost is the system call, not the interpreter': on the direct path, 20.5 of the 36.0 ms per tick (57%) is spent after the snapshot. The baseline's deltas, attribution and totals alone cost 84.5 - 74.6 = 9.9 ms per 300 processes. On Linux there is no bulk call: /proc is read per process.
findings.impact: P0 cannot apply the rule mechanically. Which provider? Snapshot only, or the whole tick with the store? Which memory figure? Which machine: CI runner or the owner's PC? Each choice flips the Python-or-Rust outcome. The 10 ms threshold is a third of the active budget, so it can call for Rust while the budget is met. It also ignores the Python work after the snapshot, which by itself reaches 10 ms.
findings.proposed_change: docs/11 'When to switch the collector to Rust': replace the first two bullets with one: 'In phase 0, run the collector (snapshot, deltas, attribution and store writes) for 10 minutes on the owner's Windows machine with 300 processes, using the provider that will ship. Switch if its CPU time exceeds the budget (3% at the active interval, 1% at the idle interval) with the default cadence, or if its private bytes exceed 80 MB.' Delete the sentence 'its cost is the system call, not the interpreter'.
findings.decision_question: Should the switch test be the budget itself (whole-collector CPU against 3% and 1%, on the owner's Windows PC), or should the 10 ms snapshot rule stay? Recommendation: the budget. On this Linux machine the measured numbers say Python meets it only with the direct reader plus a reduced per-tick set (0.68% with a 10% hot set), and never with psutil (9.5%).
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether docs/08 or docs/17 define 'full sample' more precisely: docs/17 says only 'Measure the cost of one full sample in phase 0'. The memory figures are measured as resident, unique and proportional. All are far under 80 MB, so the memory branch never decides on Linux.

findings.title: The leak acceptance sits on or above the default threshold, in mixed units, and cannot be met within 2 hours
findings.evidence: docs/01:17 and docs/17 Analysis: 'growth of 50 MB an hour must be flagged within two hours'. core/config.py:121 min_slope = 50 * 1024**2 / 3600, and core/units.py:56 'Units are binary'. growth_acceptance.out.txt, using the baseline's check_growth: section 2, no noise, 121 buckets: '50 MiB/h FLAGGED', '50 MB/h decimal growth is below the threshold'. Section 3, share of 2-h windows flagged at noise 5/30/100 MB: 50 MB decimal 0%/15%/28%; 50 MiB 45%/44%/38%; 55 MiB 100%/97%/61%. Section 1: a clean 100 MiB/h leak is flagged only with 121 buckets spanning 120 min; 'bucket 121 ... ends at 2 h 01 min and is final 30 s later' (docs/17:123 'A bucket is final 30 seconds after it ends'). Section 5: the window is unstated; a 100 MiB/h leak that starts after 6 flat hours is flagged after 1.00 h with a sliding 2 h window and 6.00 h with a growing window; at 60 MiB/h the growing window never flags in 10 h.
findings.impact: Job 3's acceptance and the P3 trigger fixture fail as written. A load generator leaking 50 MB/h is never flagged. At 50 MiB/h it is a coin flip. Even a fast leak cannot be flagged before 2 h 1.5 min. The detection delay ranges from 1 h to never, depending on a window choice the brief does not make.
findings.proposed_change: docs/01 Job 3 and docs/17 Analysis: state the acceptance in MiB, as a rate clearly above min_slope, and as 'within 2.5 hours'. Alternatively lower core/config.py Leak.min_slope (for example to 30 MiB/h) and keep '50 MiB an hour within 2.5 hours'. docs/17 Analysis: name the window (the last 2 hours of minute buckets) and the per-bucket statistic used (min or mean of private bytes). Rerun docs/review/probes/b-measurement/growth_acceptance.py to confirm.
findings.cost: Three sentences in docs and one default in config.py.
findings.decision_question: Should the acceptance move (to 100 MiB/h within 2.5 h, or 50 MiB/h at a lower threshold), or should the threshold move? Recommendation: lower min_slope to about 30 MiB/h, state 50 MiB/h within 2.5 h, and pair this with the plateau fix so that warm-ups stay cleared.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/ for a definition of MB: the glossary has none, and units.py makes settings binary. I checked whether check_growth could use a partial last bucket: it takes plain series, and docs/17:123 makes a bucket final only after 30 s. Noise-free runs reproduce exactly.

findings.title: The plateau test falsely flags the brief's own cache warm-up under the brief's own noise, and misses staircase leaks
findings.evidence: analysis/growth.py:157-165: plateau when the slope of the last third is under 0.25 x the overall slope; with minute buckets that third holds only 40 points. growth_acceptance.out.txt section 9, the docs/07:104 browser curve (0.9 GiB, tau 0.35 h). 12-h runs with at least one false leak flag: 'noise 30 MB: sliding 21 of 60 runs, growing 5 of 12'; 'noise 40 MB: sliding 34 of 60 runs, growing 6 of 12'; noise 5 MB: 0. docs/07:104 gives this browser 'noise of up to 0.04 GB either way'. Section 6: '+256 MiB every 120 min (128 MiB/h): flagged in 0 of 121 checks (never)'; '+128 MiB every 60 min: flagged in 40 of 121, levelled off in 81'. Section 8: a slow warm-up with tau 4 h is flagged in 65/121 checks (sliding) and 121/121 (growing). Section 7: a GC sawtooth with no leak (600 MiB freed every 3 h) is flagged in 107/121.
findings.impact: 'A cache warming up is not flagged' (docs/01 Job 3) fails in over half of runs with the brief's own example. The P3 quiet fixture will pass if the builder uses a noise-free warm-up, so the gate hides this. Leaks that grow in steps, such as pools that double or batch caches, read as 'levelled off'. This is R11's fix, still incomplete.
findings.proposed_change: Plan a task: replace the ratio test in growth.py plateaued() with an absolute one, so that the tail slope must itself clear min_slope (or a lower confidence bound must). Make the window span at least two steps of a staircase. docs/17 Analysis fixture list: add a warm-up with noise of at least 40 MB, a staircase leak (trigger) and a GC sawtooth (quiet), all on the minute tier. docs/15 P3 and docs/17 phase 3 list different fixtures (docs/15 names the cache warm-up, docs/17 phase 3 does not); make them match.
findings.cost: A few lines of fixture wording in docs/17 and docs/15 now; the detector change and tuning as one planned task.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked that the false flags come from the first windows, which include the rise. They do (first flag at 2.00 h), and that is realistic for a browser started under the collector. For pure noise on a flat series the 2-h Theil-Sen slope cannot reach 50 MiB/h (standard error about 3 MB/h), so the mechanism is the noisy 40-point tail slope against 25% of a moderate overall slope. The GC sawtooth case is arguable, since a 2-h window cannot tell it from a leak, so it is supporting evidence only.

findings.title: The slow-growth check cannot fire: no threshold of its own, and a 7-day window spans only 6 days of daily minimums
findings.evidence: core/config.py:124-125 SlowGrowth has only window = 7 days; there is no slope setting. baseline_table.out.txt section 3, 10 MiB/h for 7 days on hourly buckets with the baseline's daily_minimums() and check_growth(): 'window starts at midnight: 7 daily minimums spanning 6 days, leak.min_slope: flagged=False, not enough data yet'; the same with no threshold; 'window starts at 09:00: 8 daily minimums spanning 7 days, leak.min_slope: flagged=False, growth is below the threshold'; with no threshold: 'flagged=True'.
findings.impact: R34's fix ('A second check fits the daily minimum over at least 7 days') does not work as configured. If the check reuses leak.min_slope (50 MiB/h), it rejects every leak it exists to catch. With a day-aligned 7-day window it never has enough span. The P3 fixture 'a leak too slow for the hourly check' fails with the defaults.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/core/config.py SlowGrowth: add min_slope (for example 5 MiB/h, below Leak.min_slope) and define the length as at least 7 daily minimums rather than a 7-day span (or set window to 8 days). docs/17 Analysis 'Slow growth': state both values. Add a test with a 10 MiB/h leak over 8 days.
findings.cost: About 6 lines in config.py, one sentence in docs/17, one test.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/07, docs/08 and docs/17 for a slow-growth threshold: none is given. I tried both window alignments; only the 8-minimum case with no threshold flags.

findings.title: Baseline anomaly: the docs/07 table matches neither the stated rule nor usual_range(), there is no floor default, and on minute buckets 4% of ordinary minutes are flagged
findings.evidence: docs/07:116 'The deviation is never taken as less than 0.03 GB' (floor on the MAD, half-width 4 x 1.4826 x 0.03 = 0.178). analysis/growth.py:210 applies the floor to the scaled spread (half-width 0.120). baseline_table.out.txt: with the floor on the deviation, 11 of 23 ranges differ from the table by more than 0.015 GB; with the code's floor, 19 of 23 differ, and day 14 (3.30) is flagged where the table says 'within usual range' ('days flagged: [14, 23, ...]'). growth.py:203 default floor=0.0, and config.py:128-131 Baseline has no floor: 'a steady series with the default floor: (3.4, 3.4, 3.4)'. docs/17 Analysis says baselines are 'computed from minute buckets', while docs/07 shows daily peaks. On minute buckets, cores lognormal(0.5, 0.8): '61 of 1440 ordinary minutes fall outside'.
findings.impact: A builder cannot reproduce the illustrative table. With the shipped default, an idle workload with a steady value gets a zero-width range, which is the near-zero-spread problem R11 claims to have fixed. On minute buckets of a skewed CPU series, about 60 false anomalies a day per workload.
findings.proposed_change: docs/07 and the usual_range docstring: say which quantity the floor bounds, and regenerate the table from usual_range(). core/config.py Baseline: add per-metric floors (cores, memory bytes) with non-zero defaults. docs/17 Analysis: name the statistic baselined (for example hourly p95 or daily peak, built from minute buckets) and require an anomaly to persist, for example for 3 consecutive values.
findings.cost: About 10 lines across docs/07, docs/17 and config.py.
findings.refutation_attempt: I tried both floor readings and the daily-peak series exactly as the table prints it; neither reproduces it. The lognormal shape is an assumption, chosen to match the baseline's histogram test; memory with normal noise gives 1 of 1440, so the problem is specific to skewed metrics.

findings.title: The reconciliation invariant has undefined terms, the baseline tests a tautology, and the invariant fails for polled spawn loads
findings.evidence: docs/17:98 'attributed plus unattributed plus system plus restricted plus idle CPU time equals total capacity within 2%'. attribution/rules.py:36 SYSTEM is defined and never assigned. tests/test_baseline.py:268-271 checks only the sum over workloads against the sum over processes. reconcile_terms.out.txt (30.5 s, 8 cores, load 1.86): busy 53.96 CPU-s (22.12% of capacity); credited to processes 48.98; kernel threads 0.53; interrupts 0.29; 'busy time that no process accounts for 4.98 CPU-s = 2.04% of capacity'; 'System as a remainder ... the invariant is exact by definition'; 'System from counters ... leaving 1.92% of capacity for the 2% tolerance'. measure/reconcile_under_spawn.out.txt: one spawner 'missing 18.55 CPU-s = 13.7% of capacity'; four spawners 'missing 71.28 CPU-s = 51.6% of capacity'. docs/10:83 accepts about 70% undercount of polled children on Windows.
findings.impact: If System is the remainder, the invariant cannot fail, and unseen child CPU (up to 82% of busy time here) is shown as 'System' beside a 'Reconciled' bar (docs/03:43). If System comes from counters, the invariant sits at 1.92% of 2% on a quiet machine and fails by 7 to 26 times under polled spawn load, which docs/10 accepts. Either way the P1 gate 'totals reconcile within 2%' is either meaningless or fails.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17 Attribution: define idle from per-core idle counters, and system as kernel threads plus interrupt and DPC counters. Add a sixth, always-visible term, 'not seen by polling' = busy - (processes + system), shown beside polled workloads. State the 2% check as: the six terms sum to capacity, and on the quiet P1 fixture 'not seen' stays under a stated share. Replace the baseline test with one that uses SampleBatch.cpu_busy_s and logical_cores.
findings.cost: Four sentences in docs/17, a few lines in docs/03's example, and one test rewritten.
findings.decision_question: Should CPU time that polling never saw get its own visible bucket (so the invariant holds and the gap is shown), or should it go into System (the invariant holds trivially and the gap is hidden), or should the invariant be allowed to fail when polled workloads spawn? Recommendation: its own bucket.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/ for where unseen CPU goes: nothing says. I checked docs/12 for definitions of System and Idle: there are none. The Linux numbers are measured; the Windows split (interrupt and DPC) is not, but psutil's Windows cpu_times takes interrupt and dpc from per-CPU times (.venv psutil/_pswindows.py:258-269).

findings.title: Recovering reaped children from the parent's child-time counters double counts time polling already credited
findings.evidence: docs/17 Collection: 'On Linux, recover reaped children's CPU time from the parent's child-time counters.' man7 proc_pid_stat(5): cutime is 'Amount of time that this process's waited-for children have been scheduled in user mode'. man7 getrusage(2), RUSAGE_CHILDREN: 'These statistics will include the resources used by grandchildren, and further removed descendants, if all of the intervening descendants waited on their terminated children.' reconcile_terms.out.txt: 'parents' child-time counters rose by 6.76 CPU-s (gross)', against 'busy time that no process accounts for 4.98 CPU-s'. Credited plus recovered = 48.98 + 6.76 = 55.74 > 53.96 busy, so 1.78 CPU-s (3.3% of busy) would be invented.
findings.impact: A reaped child's whole lifetime goes into its parent's counter, including the part polling credited while it was alive. A grandchild's time is added again at each level that reaps. Added naively, workloads are charged more CPU than the machine used, which breaks docs/17's 'never ... invents CPU time'.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17 Collection, replace the sentence with: 'On Linux, recover only the unseen part: for each parent, its child-time increase minus the CPU last credited to children seen exiting under it, including their own child-time at last sight. Never recover more than busy time minus credited time for the interval.' Add a test fixture with nested reaping.
findings.cost: Two sentences now; the implementation is part of the P1 provider work.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether the excess could come from first sightings (credited from birth with 1 s slack): those total 0.48 CPU-s, less than the 1.78 excess. Tick rounding is about 0.01 s per process per read. The kernel definitions quoted say the counter is a lifetime total, so the overlap is structural.

findings.title: The hourly-tier gate (0.1%) depends on an unstated assignment convention, and a 30-minute soak never completes an hour bucket
findings.evidence: store/rollup.py:110 assigns each sample wholly to the bucket holding taken_at - interval/2. rollup_conventions.out.txt, hour tier against a raw sum of samples whose end time falls in the hour: 1 s '6 of 22 hours differ by more than 0.1%, worst 0.452%'; idle 5 s worst 0.788%; battery 10 s 3.186%; 30 s 6.924%; 60 s 18.698% (and 11 empty minute buckets). Against merged minutes: worst 7e-12%. 'a 30-minute soak covers at most 50% of one hour bucket ... a bucket is final 30 s after its hour ends'.
findings.impact: The P1 gate passes trivially if 'raw sum' is computed the rollup's way, and fails at every allowed cadence if raw samples are summed by their timestamps. Per-hour CPU-hours shift by up to one interval of CPU at each boundary. The CI soak cannot exercise a finished hour bucket unless the test controls the clock.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/rollup.py: split a sample across bucket edges in proportion to its overlap, so that any window's raw sum matches the tier at every cadence. docs/17 phase 1 gate: 'over the soak's whole span, using an injected clock so that at least one hour bucket closes'.
findings.cost: About 12 lines in rollup.py plus a test, and one sentence in docs/17.
findings.refutation_attempt: Merged minutes reproduce exactly, so the rollup arithmetic is correct. The gap is the convention. I checked docs/06 and docs/17 Store for a stated assignment rule: there is none.

findings.title: P1's 5% gate and P2's 2% gate compare a figure with its own source
findings.evidence: docs/17 phase 1: 'per-process figures agree with kernel counters (performance counters on Windows, /proc on Linux) within 5%'. The Linux provider reads /proc/PID/stat through psutil (.venv psutil/_pslinux.py create_time and cpu_times use _parse_stat_file). docs/17 phase 2: 'charged within 2% of the kernel's total', and the providers.group design reads that same Job Object or cgroup total. Resolution: reconcile_terms.out.txt 'one tick is 10 ms; hot threshold 0.5% of a core over 1 s is 0.5 tick, so the smallest use that can be seen in one second is 1% of a core; over 250 ms it is 4%'. man7 proc_pid_stat(5): utime is 'measured in clock ticks'.
findings.impact: Neither gate can fail except through a copying bug, so neither verifies measurement. Over a 1 s interval, any process under 10% of a core has a rounding error above 5%, so a literal per-process, per-tick reading of the P1 gate fails for unrelated reasons. The default hot_cpu_threshold (0.5%) is below one tick per second, so a process at that threshold flips in and out of the hot set.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17 phase 1 and phase 2: name independent references. On Linux, schedstat run time in nanoseconds (present here) or cgroup cpu.stat usage_usec. For both OSes, the load generator's known CPU burn, and the sum of times its children report at exit (getrusage or GetProcessTimes inside the child). Compare over at least 60 s for processes above 10% of a core. docs/08: raise the hot_cpu_threshold minimum to 1%, or evaluate it over the 10 s cold interval.
findings.cost: Two sentences in docs/17 and one table cell in docs/08.
findings.refutation_attempt: R10 replaced Task Manager with kernel counters but did not require independence. On Windows the PDH Process counters and the bulk snapshot both derive from per-process kernel times, so that part is suspected rather than shown.

findings.title: The verdict rules in docs/02 and docs/07 disagree, 'Inconclusive when signals disagree' cannot be tested, and the thermal rule fires on any turbo CPU
findings.evidence: docs/07:175-182: CPU-bound 'CPU time above 85%' plus run queue; Memory-bound 'Commit above 85% ... page writes rising'; Thermal 'below 80% of maximum under load'; Inconclusive 'Signals disagree'. docs/02:67-77: 'first match wins', Thermal checked first with 'Frequency below 80% of maximum' (no 'under load'); CPU 86% with hysteresis to 80%; Memory 86%/82% with no page-write condition; no I/O, GPU or Inconclusive rows; 'Memory tightening' and 'No bottleneck' added. This machine: cpuinfo_max_freq 4800000, base_frequency 1800000 (37.5% of max), current per-CPU 0.60-1.28 GHz at light load. docs.kernel.org intel_pstate: 'One important property of turbo P-states is that they are not sustainable.' and 'the maximum P-state that can be set for them generally depends on the number of cores running concurrently.'
findings.impact: A builder gets two rule sets. A first-match order never yields Inconclusive, and 'disagree' is undefined, so Job 2's acceptance has no test. With 'maximum' taken as the turbo maximum, docs/02's thermal rule (checked first, no load condition) reads 'Thermally throttled' at idle and under any sustained all-core load on this laptop.
findings.proposed_change: docs/07: make its table the only rule set, and have docs/02 point to it. Define maximum as base frequency (or the sustained all-core frequency measured in P0) and keep 'under load'. Define disagree as two or more verdict rules matching, or a matching rule whose ruled-out condition holds, and say that then the verdict is Inconclusive. Keep the hysteresis from docs/02.
findings.cost: About 8 lines across docs/07 and docs/02.
findings.refutation_attempt: I checked whether docs/02 is only the mock's simulation: it says 'The numbers inside the evidence follow the simulation', but the rule table itself is presented as how the verdict is chosen. The Windows meaning of maximum frequency (for example the Processor Information counters) was not verified.

findings.title: P0's WSL and Docker decision rule has no denominator, and it and the VRAM check need the owner's machine for a working day
findings.evidence: docs/15:9 'The share of CPU time held by a WSL2 or Docker VM is reported'; docs/15:45 'Phase 0 reports the VM's share of CPU time over a working day. Above 10%, the guest collector moves'. docs/17:264 the same. docs/15:9 'Per-process VRAM is checked against the adapter total'. On this machine busy time was 22% of capacity (reconcile_terms), so 10% of busy time and 10% of capacity differ by about 4.5 times.
findings.impact: 'The rule applies itself' is false: the result depends on whether the share is of busy time or of capacity. A coding agent on CI runners has no GPU, no WSL VM and no working day, so P0's gate cannot be closed by the builder.
findings.proposed_change: docs/15 'Decisions made' row and P0 gate: 'share of the machine's busy CPU time (or of capacity: pick one) held by the VM process, over at least 8 hours of normal use, measured by a script the builder supplies and the owner runs; the VRAM drift check likewise'.
findings.decision_question: Should the 10% be measured against busy CPU time or against total capacity? Recommendation: busy time, because the question is how much of the work happens out of view.
findings.refutation_attempt: I searched docs/ for 'working day' and 'share of CPU': only docs/15 and docs/17 mention them, without a denominator. R10 assigns the 24-hour soak to the owner, not the P0 measurements.

findings.title: Suspend detection on Windows may rest only on the 30 s threshold
findings.evidence: sampler.py:55 detects a suspend from wall - monotonic > 2 s, or elapsed > 30 s. docs.python.org time.monotonic: 'On Windows, call QueryPerformanceCounter() and QueryPerformanceFrequency().' The page does not say whether that clock advances during sleep. platform-check.txt: 'Whether the monotonic clock counts time asleep cannot be tested from a script'.
findings.impact: If the Windows clock advances during sleep, wall - monotonic stays near 0 across a suspend, so only the 30 s rule catches it. Fixing the first finding by raising or removing that rule would then leave Windows suspends unmarked. Rates would stay correct, because deltas are cumulative, but coverage would count sleep as observed time.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17 Collection: on Windows, detect a suspend from the power resume notification or from a clock that excludes sleep, and test it in P0's capability probe.
findings.cost: One sentence and one P0 probe.
findings.refutation_attempt: I found no Microsoft or Python statement in the pages fetched that settles whether QueryPerformanceCounter includes sleep, so the finding stays suspected.
findings.would_confirm: On the Windows 11 machine: python -c "import time;m,w=time.monotonic(),time.time();input('sleep the PC for 2 minutes, wake, press Enter');print(time.monotonic()-m, time.time()-w)". If the two figures are equal, monotonic counts sleep and the wall-minus-monotonic test never fires on Windows.
